systeme:
Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}
contenu:
Vérification des sources complémentaires : avant de rédiger, vérifie que chaque SOURCE numérotée à partir de 2 traite bien du MÊME fait que la SOURCE 1 (même événement, mêmes acteurs). Ignore entièrement celles qui n'en traitent pas et donne leurs numéros dans « sources_ecartees ». Si, sans elles, la matière ne suffit pas pour un article fiable, réponds seulement {"insuffisant": true, "titre": "…", "texte": "…"} : une brève en français (titre de 90 caractères au plus, 2 à 3 phrases d'environ 450 caractères), uniquement d'après la SOURCE 1.
Format : long
Limite de longueur : 4500 caractères au total.
Édition numérique, lue sur téléphone, sans contrainte de page : la limite suit la matière disponible dans la source. Adapte le nombre de sections à la longueur : 2 sections sous 2 000 caractères, 3 ou 4 jusqu'à 3 500, 4 à 6 au-delà ; même règle de longueur (90 à 100 % de la limite). N'étire jamais une source mince : mieux vaut un article court et exact.
Le texte réunit plusieurs sources sur le même sujet (SOURCE 1, SOURCE 2…). Croise-les sans rien ajouter ; si elles divergent, dis-le en nommant la source.
Source : TechCrunch
Rubrique : IA
Date du flux : 25/11/2026
Auteur : Sarah Perez
Titre d'origine : Character.AI’s plan to auction off users’ private chats challenged by state AGs

ARTICLE :
SOURCE 1 (TechCrunch) :
What happens to your private conversations when an AI company goes bankrupt? If it’s Character.ai, apparently, the plan is to auction them off to the highest bidder.
Now, a coalition of 42 state attorneys general is intervening in Character.ai’s bankruptcy proceedings in an effort to stop the chatbot maker from selling off sensitive user data, which includes the private conversations of millions of users.
The attorneys general involved in the matter have put out individual press releases, claiming that Character.ai’s dataset includes chat histories from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, more than 2.1 million of which belong to minors. In addition, the sale would involve other personal data, like IP addresses, the statements said.
Character.ai, which filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October, previously told consumers that their personal information would not be sold, the statements also noted. (In a blog post, Character.ai assured its users that their information would still be protected under its privacy policy.)
Only one anonymous bidder for the chat data has been disclosed so far: Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC (Smirks), which was set up as a Delaware company on November 13, 2026. The following day, Character.ai picked it as the base bid for the auction, scheduled for December 1, California Attorney General Rob Bonta noted. It is unclear what the buyer’s plans are for the chats.
The AGs are opposing this sale on the grounds that there are no protections for users — whoever buys the data can do as they like, including reselling the data without disclosure, they said. Buyers also won’t have to honor Character.ai’s privacy policy. Plus, Character.ai hasn’t provided the court with as much information as the bidders have been given about any potential safety or legal issues following the sale, the AGs claim.
In addition, some states, including California, Colorado, New York, and Connecticut, have enacted chatbot safety legislation that will go into effect on January 1, 2027, which could trigger further violations if the sale goes through.
“Character.AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold. This kind of behavior is illegal under federal and California law and bankruptcy should not be used to sidestep these consumer protections,” Bonta said in a statement.
Connecticut Attorney General William Tong also criticized Character.ai’s business model.
“Their chatbots drove vulnerable youth down a rabbit hole of emotionally volatile and sexually inappropriate chats,” Tong said. “Their reckless misconduct and broken business model drove their company into the ground. Now they want to abuse the bankruptcy process to do exactly what they said they wouldn’t do — auction off those private chat records and personal details to a shady buyer.”
Tong added: “We objected to the Disney sale, and we’re calling on the bankruptcy court to reject this sale too as yet another guise to eviscerate legal liability and consumer protection.”
The opposition to the Disney sale was led by a similar but not identical coalition of state AGs. They fought against a proposed $20 million licensing deal that would give Disney access to Character.ai’s intellectual property, but not to users’ chats. The deal has not yet received final court approval. (Disney also agreed to hire most of Character.ai’s remaining staff.)
Character.ai suffered after its co-founders, Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, returned to Google, when the tech giant signed a non-exclusive license to use the AI startup’s tech. The company also faced lawsuits related to child safety — one involved the suicide of a 14-year-old Florida boy whose mother claimed he had become obsessed with a chatbot on the platform.
California AG Bonta is joined in the effort to oppose the sale of Character.ai user data by attorneys general from Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado, Connecticut, the District of Columbia, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and West Virginia.

SOURCE 2 (Colorado Attorney General (.gov)) :
Attorney General Weiser challenges auction of millions of private Character.AI conversations
Nov. 25, 2026 (DENVER) – Attorney General Phil Weiser joined a bipartisan coalition of attorneys general challenging Character.AI’s plan to auction off its platform and the private chat histories of more than 21 million U.S. accounts, including more than 2.1 million registered to minors, without adequate privacy protections.
Scheduled for Dec. 1, the auction would include users’ private conversations, IP addresses, location information, and other sensitive data. Under the proposed sale terms, the buyer would have no obligation to honor users’ requests to delete their information or restrict how their data is used.
“Children and families who shared their most personal thoughts with Character.AI never imagined those conversations could be auctioned off to the highest bidder,” Attorney General Weiser said. “A company’s financial troubles do not give it the right to disregard its responsibility to protect consumers, especially children. Colorado is standing up to ensure that sensitive personal information is protected and that technology companies are held accountable under the law.”
In October, Attorney General Weiser led a coalition of attorneys general in raising concerns about Character.AI’s safety and privacy practices in its bankruptcy proceedings. The states called for protections for children and consumers in any sale of the company’s assets and reserved their right to challenge future transactions. Last week, Colorado and a bipartisan coalition objected to a separate license sale to Disney. The latest filing challenges the proposed sale of nearly all of Character.AI’s remaining assets.
Among the information being sold are conversations in which AI characters engaged children and adults in sexually explicit discussions, as well as exchanges where users shared intimate details about self-harm, eating disorders, and suicidal thoughts with chatbots posing as therapists, physicians, and other trusted advisors. These conversations are linked to users’ profiles and identifying information.
The states’ concerns
The coalition raises five concerns about the proposed sale:
- No protections for users. The buyer would not have to follow Character.AI’s privacy policies, honor requests to delete personal information, or limit how the data is used.
- The data could be sold again. The buyer could transfer or resell users’ information without notifying consumers, the states, or the court.
- Bidders know more than the court. Character.AI has disclosed information about its safety failures and potential legal liabilities to bidders but not to the court, states, or users.
- Potential violations of consumer protection laws. Character.AI’s chatbot service may violate state laws prohibiting unfair and deceptive practices. Additional chatbot safety laws in Colorado and several other states take effect Jan. 1, 2027.
- An anonymous lead bidder. Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC was established Nov. 13, just one day before Character.AI selected it as the opening bidder. Its investors remain undisclosed, including potential foreign investors whose identities would be shared only with Character.AI. The agreement would also require the buyer to hire only one Character.AI employee: the company’s top lawyer, despite the company’s assertion that the bidder has no ties to it.
Attorney General Weiser and the coalition argue that bankruptcy does not exempt Character.AI from federal and state consumer protection laws, including restrictions on sharing children’s personal information. Character.AI’s own privacy policy told users, “we do not sell personal information for monetary consideration.”
The states are asking the court to deny the proposed sale terms, reject Smirks as the lead bidder and deny its proposed $350,000 “break-up fee,” a payment it would collect if Character.AI ends up selling to someone else. At a minimum, the coalition argues that any sale must exclude children’s conversations and other sensitive information and include enforceable privacy protections.
The attorneys general of Colorado, California, and Connecticut are leading this effort alongside a group of states working in coordination with the National Association of Attorneys General. Also joining the filing are the attorneys general of Alaska, Arkansas, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin, West Virginia, and the District of Columbia.
